updates.title: The three new criminal laws are now in force
updates.summary: BNS, BNSS and BSA replaced the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act with effect from 1 July 2024.
body: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024, replacing the Indian Penal Code, 1860, the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 respectively.
Offences committed before 1 July 2024 continue to be governed by the IPC. Investigations, inquiries and trials pending on that date are saved by S. 531 BNSS.
Key procedural features include Zero FIR and e-FIR (S. 173 BNSS), videography of search and seizure, and timelines for investigation and judgment.

updates.title: Arrest in offences punishable up to 7 years — what the law requires
updates.summary: The police must satisfy the necessity of arrest; a notice of appearance is the norm.
body: In Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar, (2014) 8 SCC 273, the Supreme Court held that arrest in offences punishable with imprisonment up to seven years cannot be routine; the officer must record reasons satisfying the conditions now contained in S. 35(1)(b) BNSS.
Where arrest is not required, a notice of appearance must be issued under S. 35(3) BNSS [S. 41A CrPC]. Magistrates must not authorise detention mechanically.
Non-compliance can expose the officer to departmental action and contempt.

updates.title: Cheque dishonoured? The 30-day rule you must not miss
updates.summary: The demand notice must be sent within 30 days of receiving the bank's return memo.
body: Under proviso (b) to S. 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the payee must make a written demand within 30 days of receiving information of dishonour from the bank.
The drawer then has 15 days from receipt of the notice to pay. A complaint filed before the 15 days expire is premature — Yogendra Pratap Singh v. Savitri Pandey, (2014) 10 SCC 713.
The complaint must be filed within one month of the cause of action (S. 142(1)(b)). Use the Cheque Bounce calculator under “Tools” to work out your dates.

updates.title: Anticipatory bail under S. 482 BNSS is not time-bound
updates.summary: Protection ordinarily continues till the end of trial unless limited by the court.
body: A Constitution Bench in Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi), (2020) 5 SCC 1, held that protection granted under S. 438 CrPC (now S. 482 BNSS) need not be limited to a fixed period and does not end at the filing of the charge-sheet, unless the court for specific reasons so directs.
Applications may be moved before the Sessions Court or the High Court, which have concurrent jurisdiction.
